## The twelve cards
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Twelve regions, one structure: the system, who decides, the main challenges, what researchers ask, key numbers with their sources, and the date they were read. The cards describe; none ranks regions or judges a policy.</p>
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="regions" data-src="../assets/learn/data/regions.json">
<div class="lx-fallback"><p class="lx-hint">All twelve cards are below; with JavaScript on, a filter shows them by dominant scale.</p></div>
</div>

<ul class="rg-tiles"><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#us"><b>United States</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>interconnection queues · large-load adequacy</i></a></li><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#plains"><b>The Plains (SPP region)</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>wind · winter adequacy</i></a></li><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#eu"><b>European Union</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>market coupling · flexibility</i></a></li><li data-scale="national"><a href="#china"><b>China</b><span>Nation</span><i>curtailment · ultra-high-voltage lines</i></a></li><li data-scale="national"><a href="#india"><b>India</b><span>Nation</span><i>evening peak · distribution-company finances</i></a></li><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#japan-korea"><b>Japan and South Korea</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>import dependence · links between regions</i></a></li><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#nordics"><b>Nordic countries</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>hydro and wind · bidding zones</i></a></li><li data-scale="national"><a href="#gulf"><b>Gulf states</b><span>Nation</span><i>cooling peaks · power and water</i></a></li><li data-scale="microgrid"><a href="#ssa"><b>Sub-Saharan Africa</b><span>Microgrid and local</span><i>energy access · power pools</i></a></li><li data-scale="national"><a href="#latam"><b>Latin America</b><span>Nation</span><i>hydro and climate risk · curtailment</i></a></li><li data-scale="microgrid"><a href="#islands"><b>Small island systems</b><span>Microgrid and local</span><i>imported fuel · low inertia</i></a></li><li data-scale="regional"><a href="#australia"><b>Australia</b><span>Regional grid</span><i>rooftop solar · minimum demand</i></a></li></ul>
<!-- regions-tiles:end -->
<div class="rg-list">
<!-- regions-cards:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="us" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>United States</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · interconnection queues · large-load adequacy</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Seven ISO/RTO markets, plus vertically integrated utilities in much of the Southeast and West.</li><li>Three weakly coupled interconnections.</li><li>Gas is the largest source of electricity; demand is rising again with data centers, manufacturing and electrification.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>FERC: wholesale markets and interstate transmission.</li><li>NERC: reliability standards.</li><li>DOE and EIA: research, policy and statistics.</li><li>State utility commissions: retail rates.</li><li>ISOs and RTOs: grid operation and markets.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>A long interconnection backlog, and who pays for new transmission.</li><li>Adequacy as large loads arrive and older plants retire.</li><li>Extreme weather.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How much capacity can flexible large loads save?</li><li>Do the cluster-study reforms after FERC Order 2023 shorten the time to operation?</li><li>What does transmission between regions buy in extreme cold?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>About 2,061 GW seeking interconnection at the end of 2025: 1,312 GW of generation and about 749 GW of storage. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/publications/queued-2026-edition-characteristics">Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, May 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Wind and utility-scale solar made 17% of 2025's generation; 19% with small-scale solar. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67367">U.S. Energy Information Administration, 20 March 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Data centers used 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023 (176 TWh). <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-increase-electricity-demand-data-centers">U.S. Department of Energy, 20 December 2024</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="plains" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>The Plains (SPP region)</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · wind · winter adequacy</p></header><p class="lx-hint rg-note">Prairie Town's real-data home: the course's hourly shapes come from this grid.</p><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>A regional transmission organization (RTO): it runs the bulk grid and the wholesale market for its members.</li><li>One market since 1 March 2014, the Integrated Marketplace: day-ahead and real-time energy, reserves and congestion rights.</li><li>At the western edge of the Eastern Interconnection, between MISO to the east and ERCOT to the south.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>SPP: reliability coordination, scheduling, transmission planning and the wholesale market.</li><li>FERC: granted SPP its RTO status in 2004.</li><li>SPP's Market Monitoring Unit: an independent monitor that reports on the market each year.</li><li>Members: generation-and-transmission cooperatives, municipal systems, investor-owned utilities, independent transmission companies and power producers.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Congestion and wind curtailment: average hourly curtailment rose from 136 MW in 2019 to 1,097 MW in 2023.</li><li>Winter adequacy and fuel supply: in February 2021 SPP cut regional demand twice, the first region-wide curtailments in its history.</li><li>In 2025, rising gas prices, load growth and resource adequacy concerns.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How much does new transmission cut wind curtailment and congestion?</li><li>How should capacity be accredited when cold weather takes out many plants and their fuel at once?</li><li>How should wind forecast uncertainty enter the day-ahead commitment?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>161 members in all or part of 17 states, about 732,086 square miles; among them 26 generation-and-transmission cooperatives, 18 municipal systems and 16 investor-owned utilities. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/">Southwest Power Pool, updated October 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Wind made 36.7% of the 300,382 GWh produced in 2025, more than coal (29%) or gas (25.1%). <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/">Southwest Power Pool, updated October 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Wind capacity 35,934 MW at the end of 2025. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.spp.org/documents/76798/2025_annual_state_of_the_market_report.pdf">Southwest Power Pool, 27 May 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Peak 58.0 GW on 27 July 2026, a record; the earlier peak was 56.0 GW on 21 August 2023. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68305">U.S. Energy Information Administration, 15 October 2026</a>)</span></li><li>February 2021: demand cut by about 1.5% for 50 minutes on 15 February and about 6.5% for about three hours on 16 February. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://spp.org/documents/65038/spp%27s%20response%20to%20the%20february%202021%20winter%20weather%20event%20-%20summary.pdf">Southwest Power Pool, undated</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 7 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="eu" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>European Union</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · market coupling · flexibility</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Unbundled zonal markets, coupled day-ahead and intraday.</li><li>Dense interconnection between countries.</li><li>Nuclear power, led by France; wind; fast-growing solar.</li><li>Flat demand overall, with clusters of data-center load.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>European Commission (DG ENER): energy law and policy.</li><li>ACER: cooperation of national regulators.</li><li>ENTSO-E: the transmission operators' network and grid plans.</li><li>National regulators and TSOs; Eurostat for statistics.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Congestion and redispatch costs.</li><li>Negative prices and falling solar capture prices.</li><li>Security of supply after 2022.</li><li>Slow permitting of grids.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How does bidding-zone design affect redispatch?</li><li>Which mix of storage, demand response and interconnection cuts negative-price hours most?</li><li>Which connection rules fit clusters of data-center load?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Renewables made 47.5% of gross electricity consumption in 2024 (Austria 90.1%, Malta 10.7%). <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260114-1">Eurostat, 14 January 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Wind and solar made 30% of 2025's electricity, above fossil fuels at 29%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/european-electricity-review-2026/">Ember, 22 January 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Data centers used 23% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2025 (5% in 2015). <span class="rg-src">(Central Statistics Office, July 2026)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="china" data-scale="national"><header class="rg-head"><h3>China</h3><p class="rg-tags">Nation · curtailment · ultra-high-voltage lines</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>State-owned grid companies; dispatch largely by province.</li><li>Spot markets moving toward a unified national market; market pricing for new wind and solar since 2025.</li><li>Ultra-high-voltage (UHV) lines carry power from west to east; coal still leads generation.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>NDRC and NEA: planning, prices and energy regulation.</li><li>State Grid and China Southern Power Grid.</li><li>China Electricity Council; the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).</li><li>Beijing and Guangzhou power exchanges.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Rising curtailment of wind and solar.</li><li>Barriers to trade between provinces.</li><li>Coal plants retrofitted for flexibility, and capacity payments.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How do provincial spot designs affect how much wind and solar is used?</li><li>Which mix of UHV lines, storage and flexible coal keeps utilisation at or above 90% at least cost?</li><li>How does market pricing change where wind and solar are built?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>317 GW of solar added in 2025; utilisation 95% for solar and 94% for wind. <span class="rg-src">(National Energy Administration of China, 12 February 2026)</span></li><li>Solar capacity 1,286 GW at the end of July 2026, passing coal at 1,285 GW. <span class="rg-src">(National Energy Administration of China, 11 September 2026)</span></li><li>Fossil fuels made 58% of 2025's electricity; wind and solar 22%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/china/">Ember, read 2 November 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="india" data-scale="national"><header class="rg-head"><h3>India</h3><p class="rg-tags">Nation · evening peak · distribution-company finances</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>State distribution companies (DISCOMs) buy power under long-term contracts.</li><li>One synchronous national grid.</li><li>Coal makes most of the electricity, while most capacity is now non-fossil; the evening peak binds.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Ministry of Power and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).</li><li>Central Electricity Authority (CEA).</li><li>CERC and state commissions: regulation and tariffs.</li><li>Grid-India (operator), CTUIL (transmission planning) and SECI (renewable tenders).</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>The finances of distribution companies.</li><li>The evening peak in a solar-heavy system.</li><li>Transmission and storage for the Rajasthan and Gujarat renewable zones.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How much storage does each step in solar's share need?</li><li>How do solar-powered farm feeders and time-of-day tariffs reshape load?</li><li>Does market coupling outperform bilateral contracts?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Non-fossil capacity 300.50 GW, over 54% of about 552 GW, on 31 July 2026. <span class="rg-src">(Press Information Bureau, 9 August 2026)</span></li><li>Fossil fuels made 73% of 2025's electricity; solar 9.4%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/india/">Ember, read 2 November 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="japan-korea" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Japan and South Korea</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · import dependence · links between regions</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Japan: ten areas, split between 50 Hz and 60 Hz, joined by limited converters; liberalised retail, a power exchange (JEPX) and a capacity market.</li><li>South Korea: one network and retail company (KEPCO) and a cost-based pool (KPX).</li><li>Both are isolated systems that import their fuels; nuclear plays a large role in both.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Japan: METI and its energy agency (ANRE), OCCTO (cross-regional coordination), the Nuclear Regulation Authority, JEPX.</li><li>South Korea: the energy ministry (MOTIE), KEPCO, KPX.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Dependence on imported fuel.</li><li>Curtailment and weak links between regions (Kyushu, Jeju).</li><li>Finding sites for offshore wind.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>What would more 50/60 Hz converter capacity save?</li><li>How should South Korea plan southwest offshore wind together with lines to Seoul?</li><li>LNG storage or batteries as a hedge for supply security?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Japan, 2025: fossil fuels 67% of electricity, solar 10%, nuclear 9%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/japan/">Ember, read 2 November 2026</a>)</span></li><li>South Korea, 2025: fossil fuels 60% of electricity; wind and solar 7%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/south-korea/">Ember, updated 22 April 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="nordics" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Nordic countries</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · hydro and wind · bidding zones</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Nord Pool bidding zones; flow-based market coupling since October 2024; dense HVDC links.</li><li>Hydro in Norway and Sweden, wind in Denmark.</li><li>Sweden and Finland also run nuclear plants.</li><li>New industrial, hydrogen and data-center loads; district heating in many cities.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Grid operators: Statnett, Svenska kraftnät, Fingrid, Energinet.</li><li>National regulators.</li><li>Nord Pool: the power exchange.</li><li>Statistics Norway (SSB) and Eurostat: statistics.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>North-south congestion and price gaps.</li><li>Dry-year risk for hydro.</li><li>Inertia, and new large loads.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How has flow-based coupling changed price spreads?</li><li>How should the value of stored water be modelled as wind grows?</li><li>What flexibility can district heating give?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Norway, 2025: 161.8 TWh generated, hydro 89.9%, a record net export of 22.8 TWh. <span class="rg-src">(Statistics Norway, May 2026)</span></li><li>Renewables' share of gross electricity consumption in 2024: Sweden 88.1%, Denmark 79.7%, Finland 54.3%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260114-1">Eurostat, 14 January 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="gulf" data-scale="national"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Gulf states</h3><p class="rg-tags">Nation · cooling peaks · power and water</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Vertically integrated state utilities; single buyers contract independent power producers and power-and-water plants.</li><li>Oman runs a spot market; the GCC Interconnection Authority links all six states.</li><li>Gas and oil make most electricity, with large solar tenders.</li><li>The UAE also runs a nuclear plant.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Saudi Arabia: Ministry of Energy, the regulator SERA, Saudi Electricity Company.</li><li>UAE: Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, DEWA, EWEC.</li><li>Qatar's KAHRAMAA; Oman's regulator APSR.</li><li>The GCC Interconnection Authority (GCCIA).</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>The value of oil burned for power that could be sold.</li><li>Summer peaks driven by cooling.</li><li>Subsidised tariffs, and power and water plants that run together.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How should power and water be planned together with solar and storage?</li><li>How much peak can district cooling and thermal storage shave?</li><li>What is reserve sharing through the GCCIA worth?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Saudi Arabia: 98% of electricity from fossil fuels; demand per person 3.5 times the world average (data year not stated). <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/saudi-arabia/">Ember, updated 22 April 2026</a>)</span></li><li>UAE: 68% from fossil fuels; demand per person 4.2 times the world average (data year not stated). <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/united-arab-emirates/">Ember, updated 22 April 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="ssa" data-scale="microgrid"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Sub-Saharan Africa</h3><p class="rg-tags">Microgrid and local · energy access · power pools</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Mostly vertically integrated state utilities; Nigeria unbundled in 2013, and South Africa's Eskom is unbundling.</li><li>Thin regional power pools (SAPP, WAPP, EAPP, CAPP).</li><li>Hydro in many countries, coal in South Africa; diesel and off-grid solar where the grid does not reach.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>National utilities and regulators.</li><li>The regional power pools.</li><li>The African Development Bank, the World Bank and AUDA-NEPAD.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>The rural access gap.</li><li>Utility finances and load shedding.</li><li>Climate risk to hydro; a high cost of capital.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>Where is grid extension, a mini-grid or a solar home system the least-cost way to connect people?</li><li>What is regional trade worth when river flows vary?</li><li>Which tariffs make mini-grids viable?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>655 million people worldwide without electricity, over 560 million of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/06/16/accelerating-universal-energy-access">World Bank and the custodian agencies, 24 June 2026</a>)</span></li><li>South Africa, 2025: 83% of electricity from fossil fuels; wind and solar 13%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/south-africa/">Ember, updated 22 April 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="latam" data-scale="national"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Latin America</h3><p class="rg-tags">Nation · hydro and climate risk · curtailment</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>Brazil: a hydro-dominated national grid (the SIN), cost-based dispatch, auctions plus a free market.</li><li>Chile: liberalised, with cost-based dispatch on a grid about 3,000 km long.</li><li>Mexico: the state utility CFE dominates after the 2025 reform.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Brazil: MME, the regulator ANEEL, the operator ONS, the planner EPE, the trading chamber CCEE.</li><li>Chile: the energy commission CNE and the operator CEN.</li><li>Mexico: SENER, the operator CENACE, CFE.</li><li>OLADE, the regional energy organisation.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Drought risk to hydro.</li><li>Curtailment and transmission bottlenecks in northern Chile.</li><li>Investment uncertainty in Mexico.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How should reservoirs be run together with wind and solar under drought (stochastic dual dynamic programming)?</li><li>Which storage and transmission cut Chile's curtailment most cheaply?</li><li>How do compensation rules for rooftop and other distributed generation shift costs?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Brazil, 2025: hydro 52% of electricity, wind and solar 27%, clean sources 89%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/brazil/">Ember, updated 30 October 2026</a>)</span></li><li>Chile: 20,483.5 MW of non-conventional renewable capacity out of 39,104.4 MW installed, November 2025. <span class="rg-src">(Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional, December 2025)</span></li><li>Mexico, 2025: 74% of electricity from fossil fuels; wind and solar 13%. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/mexico/">Ember, updated 20 May 2026</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="islands" data-scale="microgrid"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Small island systems</h3><p class="rg-tags">Microgrid and local · imported fuel · low inertia</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>One integrated utility per island.</li><li>Small, isolated grids with little inertia.</li><li>Imported diesel and fuel oil; high shares of rooftop solar.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>Hawaii's Public Utilities Commission and State Energy Office.</li><li>CARICOM's Energy Unit and CCREEE (Caribbean).</li><li>The Pacific Community, PCREEE and the Pacific Power Association.</li><li>IRENA's SIDS Lighthouses initiative.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Volatile fuel costs.</li><li>Stability at very high shares of inverter-based power.</li><li>Storm resilience.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How much grid-forming capacity does a grid that runs almost entirely on inverters need?</li><li>Which mix of solar, storage and diesel holds up under fuel-price and storm risk?</li><li>How should rooftop export tariffs work once midday solar exceeds load?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Hawaii's average retail price was 38.00 cents per kWh in 2024, the highest of any state; the U.S. average was 12.94. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/state/hawaii/">U.S. Energy Information Administration, 10 November 2025</a>)</span></li><li>Hawaii had the highest average residential bill in the U.S. in 2024: $213 a month. <span class="rg-src">(<a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65244">U.S. Energy Information Administration, 12 May 2025</a>)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 2 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<article class="lx-card rg-card" id="australia" data-scale="regional"><header class="rg-head"><h3>Australia</h3><p class="rg-tags">Regional grid · rooftop solar · minimum demand</p></header><dl class="rg-parts"><div class="rg-part"><dt>System structure</dt><dd><ul><li>The National Electricity Market (NEM): one wholesale market across Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania.</li><li>Western Australia runs its own Wholesale Electricity Market.</li><li>Millions of rooftop solar systems; grid-scale batteries growing fast.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Institutions</dt><dd><ul><li>AEMO: independent market and system operator and system planner for the NEM and Western Australia's market.</li><li>The Clean Energy Regulator: runs the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme for rooftop systems, which ends in 2030.</li><li>State governments and distribution network businesses: emergency backstops that can turn rooftop solar down.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Main challenges</dt><dd><ul><li>Minimum system load on sunny, mild days, typically in autumn and spring.</li><li>Keeping enough essential system services as large spinning generators run less.</li><li>Evening peaks (4 pm to 9 pm), now partly met by batteries.</li></ul></dd></div><div class="rg-part"><dt>Distinctive research questions</dt><dd><ul><li>How can demand stay above secure minimum levels with millions of rooftop systems connected?</li><li>How do home and grid-scale batteries reshape evening peaks and prices?</li><li>Which services replace what large spinning generators gave the grid?</li></ul></dd></div></dl><div class="rg-nums"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Verified key numbers</p><ul><li>Renewables made 44.3% of NEM generation in July to September 2026, a record for that quarter (41.8% a year earlier). <span class="rg-src">(Australian Energy Market Operator, October 2026)</span></li><li>NEM-wide minimum operational demand fell to an all-time low of 9,422 MW on Sunday 20 September 2026. <span class="rg-src">(Australian Energy Market Operator, October 2026)</span></li><li>Rooftop and other distributed solar averaged 3,203 MW in July to September 2026, a record for that quarter. <span class="rg-src">(Australian Energy Market Operator, October 2026)</span></li><li>4,562,198 small-scale solar systems installed across Australia, 30,917,812 kW of rated output, as of 30 September 2026 (all of Australia, not only the NEM). <span class="rg-src">(Clean Energy Regulator, last updated 20 October 2026)</span></li></ul></div><p class="rg-asof"><b>As of 7 November 2026</b>, when each number was read on its source; each source line gives its own date.</p><p class="rg-top"><a href="#cards">Back to all regions</a></p></article>
<!-- regions-cards:end -->
</div>
```
